content: Candida vulvovaginitis is an infection that affects the vagina and the vestibule, most commonly seen in women of reproductive age. The infection is primarily caused by various species of Candida, with Candida albicans being the most frequent pathogen, followed by other species such as Candida glabrata and Candida krusei. Diagnosis of this condition requires a combination of clinical evaluation and diagnostic findings. Patients typically present with a characteristic white, cottage cheese-like vaginal discharge, and microscopy often reveals the presence of hyphae and spores. Uncomplicated infections generally respond well to treatment with topical or oral azole antifungal agents. However, 5 to 8% of women experience recurrent vulvovaginitis, defined as more than four episodes in a year. These cases require extended therapy, which includes an induction phase followed by a maintenance phase. Historically, Candida was first described in 1839 by B. Lagenbeck in Germany, who identified a yeast-like fungus in cases of oral thrush and its ability to cause infection. Candida vulvovaginitis can be classified based on the duration of the infection and the specific strain of Candida involved. The pathophysiology of the disease involves several virulence factors of Candida, but the transition from asymptomatic vaginal colonization to symptomatic vulvovaginitis remains poorly understood. Genetic predisposition may play a role, as the condition often runs in families and is more prevalent among African-American women. Other contributing factors include bacterial co-colonization, the human immune response, and external or internal disturbances that disrupt the normal vaginal flora, such as irritants, hormonal changes, or physiological imbalances. In a study of 1009 women in New Zealand, Candida albicans was isolated from the vaginas of 19% of apparently healthy women, most of whom experienced few or no symptoms. However, external irritants (e.g., detergents or douches) or internal disturbances (e.g., hormonal or physiological changes) can disrupt the normal vaginal flora, which is predominantly composed of lactic acid bacteria like lactobacilli. This disruption can lead to yeast overgrowth and symptomatic infection. Risk factors include pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, unclean practices following anal sex, and the use of glycerin-containing lubricants. Diabetes mellitus and antibiotic use are also associated with an increased risk of yeast infections. Candida infections can be sexually transmitted from men to women but not from women to men. In some cases, diet has been implicated as a cause in animal studies. Hormone replacement therapy and infertility treatments may also predispose individuals to infection. Differentiating Candida vulvovaginitis from other conditions with similar presentations, such as bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas vaginitis, and atrophic vaginitis, is essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment. Epidemiological studies on the prevalence of Candida vulvovaginitis are challenging to conduct, as it is not a reportable disease. Antibiotic use, pregnancy, diabetes, and obesity are all risk factors that create conditions favorable for yeast overgrowth. There are no current screening recommendations for Candida vulvovaginitis. The condition is generally self-limiting and does not lead to complications, although some patients may experience recurrences. It responds well to local or oral antifungal treatments. A thick, whitish vaginal discharge that adheres to the vaginal walls is a common clinical finding. Laboratory diagnosis involves examining a small sample of vaginal discharge under a microscope using a wet mount and potassium hydroxide (KOH) test. In cases where the infection does not improve with treatment or recurs frequently, a culture may be performed. Treatment involves the use of antifungal agents, such as amphotericin, clotrimazole, nystatin, fluconazole, and ketoconazole. Surgery has no role in the management of Candida vulvovaginitis, as medical therapy with topical and/or oral antifungal drugs is the primary treatment approach. Primary prevention of Candida vulvovaginitis is not well-established, but wearing cotton underwear may help reduce the risk of infection. For secondary prevention, maintenance therapy with fluconazole prophylaxis may be used to prevent recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis. Treating a male sexual partner with oral ketoconazole does not appear to influence cure or recurrence rates in women with Candida vulvovaginitis.
